references.observation: 2015 front photograph of the rebuilt arch. The left pedestal forks below the upturned crest. The broad right wing carries six visible depressions.
2016 rear photograph showing the fork through the pedestal, narrow crosspiece and thinner back of the swept wing.
The Trust distinguishes the rebuilt Flying Tortoise from the Chameleon Gate, the Obatala Complex and the Second Palace.

The wide front photograph shows the scalloped wall on the left and an opening through the right wall. A thick, rolled lip rises around the diagonal slit, and the cement flares out at ground level. Rear thickness and wall depth are estimated.
The carved shelter is the one shown alone and through the Flying Tortoise in two photos from the 2016 visit. Its geographic tag constrains the outer side of the arch.

map.note: The 2016 grove-side photo shows the roofed entrance to the sacred path past the arch’s forked pier. A geotagged photo shows the same shelter, with a swept bamboo eave, recessed plaster opening and adjoining scalloped wall, near survey point 32. The tagged camera is southwest of the arch, on the outer side beside the fork. The model faces about 211° true across the nearby PMTiles branch. The 2 m shift east of the survey point clears both mapped roads. The exact crossing and bearing are estimated.

limitations: Approximate meter scale from visitors in the photographs. Sculpture depths, concealed joints and adjoining wall extents are estimated.
